section.title: Christ the Wisdom and Power of God
section.sectionRationale: Here Paul answers the whole Corinthian obsession with wisdom and status by unfolding the paradox of the cross. The message of a crucified Messiah looks like folly and weakness to the world, yet it is the very wisdom and power of God. God deliberately overturns human standards, saving through what the world despises and choosing the lowly, so that no one may boast before Him. The section climaxes in Christ Himself, who has become for believers wisdom from God: righteousness, holiness, and redemption, leaving one boast alone, boasting in the Lord.
section.thesis: The word of the cross, foolishness and weakness to the perishing, is the wisdom and power of God to the saved; God overturns worldly wisdom and status, choosing the foolish and weak and lowly so that no flesh may boast, for Christ Himself has become our wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the word of the cross, foolishness or power; Christ crucified as the wisdom and power of God to the called; God's choice of the foolish and weak so none may boast; and Christ our wisdom, so that boasting is only in the Lord.

units.label: The word of the cross
units.note: foolishness to the perishing, power to the saved

verses.text: For the message of the cross is {{moria|foolishness}} to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the {{dynamis|power}} of God.
For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise; the intelligence of the intelligent I will frustrate.”
Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the philosopher of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?

units.label: Christ crucified, God's wisdom and power
units.note: a stumbling block and folly, yet the wisdom of God

verses.text: For since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know Him, God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe.
Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom,
but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,
but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the {{sophia|wisdom}} of God.
For the foolishness of God is wiser than man’s wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than man’s strength.

units.label: God chose the foolish and weak
units.note: so that no one may boast

verses.text: Brothers, consider the time of your calling: Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth.
But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong.
He chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and the things that are not, to nullify the things that are,
so that no one may boast in His presence.
It is because of Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and {{apolytrosis|redemption}}.
Therefore, as it is written: “Let him who boasts {{kauchaomai|boast}} in the Lord.”

moria.gloss: Foolishness, absurdity, the quality of being ridiculous. It is how the message of a crucified Messiah appears to the perishing, and the word from which we get moron. Paul takes the world's dismissive verdict and turns it on its head: this apparent folly is the saving wisdom of God, and God has made the world's own wisdom foolish.

dynamis.gloss: Power, might, effective force, the root of dynamite. The cross, which looks like weakness and defeat, is in fact the power of God that saves. Paul insists that real divine power is displayed not in worldly strength but in the crucified Christ, whose apparent weakness is stronger than all human strength.

sophia.gloss: Wisdom, skill, insight. The Greeks prized it and the Corinthians craved it, yet the world's wisdom failed to know God. In answer, Christ crucified is the true wisdom of God, and Christ Himself becomes wisdom from God for His people, exposing human cleverness as no path to God at all.

kauchaomai.gloss: To boast, to glory, to take pride in. God has arranged salvation so that boasting in oneself is excluded; the only legitimate boast is in the Lord. The Corinthian pride in wisdom, status, and favorite teachers is undone, and every ground of self-congratulation is transferred to Christ.

apolytrosis.gloss: Redemption, release secured by the payment of a ransom, the buying back of a slave or captive. Christ has become our redemption, freeing us at the cost of Himself. It joins righteousness and holiness as one of the saving benefits Christ has become for His people, so that all of salvation is found in Him and not in human achievement.

basic.context: Paul now explains why he refuses to rely on clever words. The message of the cross seems like foolishness to those perishing, but to the saved it is the power of God. God deliberately chose to save through what the world calls weak and foolish, a crucified Messiah, so that human wisdom and pride are overturned. He even chose lowly, unimpressive people, like most of the Corinthians, so that no one could boast. In the end, Christ Himself becomes everything for them, their wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption.
basic.hermeneutics: This is sustained theological argument built on the paradox of the cross and supported by Scripture, Isaiah 29 and Jeremiah 9. Paul reasons from what God did at the cross and from whom God called. The abiding truth is that salvation is God's wise and powerful work, received by faith, so that all boasting is excluded and Christ alone is glorified.
basic.originalLanguages: The cross looks like moria, foolishness, but is the dynamis, power, of God. The world's sophia, wisdom, could not find God, so God saves through what seems foolish. Christ becomes wisdom from God for us, our righteousness, holiness, and apolytrosis, redemption. The result is that the only kauchaomai, boasting, left is boasting in the Lord.
basic.typology: Christ crucified fulfills the pattern of God saving through weakness and reversal seen throughout the Old Testament, choosing the younger, the barren, the small, and the despised. Isaiah's promise to confound the wise is fulfilled at the cross. The redemption Christ becomes fulfills the ransom and release pictured in the exodus and the year of release.
basic.christ: Christ crucified is the center: a stumbling block to Jews, folly to Gentiles, but to the called the power and wisdom of God. More than that, Christ has become for believers wisdom from God, and in Him righteousness, holiness, and redemption. He does not merely give these gifts; He is them for His people.
basic.god: God is sovereign and wise beyond human measure. He deliberately overturns the world's wisdom and strength, saving through the cross and choosing the lowly, precisely so that no one can boast before Him. His foolishness is wiser than men and His weakness stronger than men, revealing a God who saves in a way that humbles all pride.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 29 promises God will destroy the wisdom of the wise. Romans says the gospel is God's power for salvation. Second Corinthians shows God's power made perfect in weakness. Jeremiah supplies the call to boast only in knowing the Lord.
basic.oneStory: Throughout the Bible God saves through reversal, lifting the lowly and confounding the proud. The cross is the climax of that pattern: the ultimate weakness that is the ultimate power, the apparent folly that is the deepest wisdom. In Christ crucified, God undoes human boasting and becomes everything His people need.

context.literary:
First Corinthians 1:18 to 31 is a carefully built argument in four steps, and the steps are linked by the word 'for,' which opens verses 18, 19, 21, 25 and 26. The paragraph begins with a thesis in verse 18, that the message of the cross divides hearers into two groups, those who are perishing and those who are being saved. Verse 19 supports it from Scripture. Verses 20 to 21 press it with a string of rhetorical questions and a statement of God's purpose. Verses 22 to 25 name the two kinds of seeker, Jews and Greeks, and show that Christ crucified answers neither of their demands on their own terms, and then turn to the called, for whom He is power and wisdom. Verses 26 to 29 move from the message to the messengers' audience, the Corinthians themselves, and ask them to look at who they were when called. Verses 30 to 31 close the circle with Christ as the source of all that they have, and a scriptural line that sends the boasting back to the Lord.

The paragraph is full of balanced pairs. Wise and foolish, strong and weak, noble and lowly, 'things that are' and 'things that are not' arrive in a rhythm that makes the reversal easy to hear. Verses 27 and 28 give the pattern three times with the same verb, 'God chose,' repeated at the start of each clause. It is a rhetorical figure, the repeated opening, that drives the point in like a hammer. The three objects, the foolish, the weak, the lowly, are matched by three purposes: to shame the wise, to shame the strong, and to nullify what is.

The central sentence, verse 25, is a pair of paradoxes in which the comparison is stretched past its natural limit. 'The foolishness of God' is not simply less wise than human wisdom, it is wiser, and 'the weakness of God' is stronger. Paul is using language that his readers would have treated as a contradiction to show that their categories fail.

Within the whole letter the paragraph belongs to chapters 1 to 4, which deal with divisions. Paul has just said, in verse 17, that the cross must not be emptied of its power by clever speech. These verses fill in what that power looks like and why it cannot be displayed through the instruments the Corinthians admire.
context.historical:
Paul wrote to a city that prized rhetoric, and the Corinthians had a social world in which status was everything. Rank was marked by birth, wealth and education, and public speech was the mark of the educated. A visiting teacher was judged by his delivery as much as by his message. In such a setting the news of a crucified Messiah was not merely unfashionable but shameful. Crucifixion was the penalty Rome used for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals, and Roman writers such as Cicero said that the very word 'cross' should be kept far from the thoughts and ears of a Roman citizen. To tell educated Corinthians that their saviour had died that way was to tell them something they would find offensive.

For Jewish hearers the offence was of a different kind. Deuteronomy 21:23 says that anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse. A Messiah who ended in that way seemed to be a contradiction, and Paul says as much when he writes in Galatians 3:13 that Christ became a curse for us. The Jews 'demand signs' in verse 22, as in the Gospels, where people ask Jesus for a sign from heaven, Matthew 12:38 and 16:1. The Greeks, by contrast, 'search for wisdom,' the pursuit of the philosophical schools, and Paul had met their questions in Athens shortly before arriving in Corinth, Acts 17:16 to 34, where the talk of a resurrection met scorn.

Verse 26 is a rare glimpse of the church's make up. 'Not many' is not 'none,' and the letters elsewhere show that there were people of means among them. Crispus had been the synagogue leader, Acts 18:8. Gaius was a host with a house large enough for the church, Romans 16:23. Erastus, named in the same verse, was the city treasurer. Most of the church, though, were of modest standing, and there were slaves among them, 7:21. Paul asks them to look at their own membership and see what kind of people God had chosen.

The quotation in verse 19 comes from Isaiah 29:14. The setting there is Jerusalem under pressure from Assyria, where leaders have been making plans in secret, Isaiah 29:15, and looking to Egypt for help, Isaiah 30:1 to 2. God answers that the wisdom of those schemers will vanish. Paul's use fits the original meaning, since political cleverness that excluded God is the Old Testament example of human wisdom failing.
context.canonical:
The paragraph rests on the Old Testament at both ends. Verse 19 quotes Isaiah 29:14, where God promises to confound a people whose worship is lip service and whose counsel is clever and godless. Verse 20 echoes Isaiah 33:18, 'Where is he who tallies? Where is he who weighs?' where the prophet looks at the fallen enemy and asks where the clever officials have gone. Verse 31 closes with a line from Jeremiah 9:24, which comes at the end of a passage that sets three things against each other, wisdom, might and wealth, and says that the only thing in which a person may boast is knowing the LORD. Paul has taken the three things in Jeremiah 9:23 and made them the three things the Corinthians admire, the wise, the powerful and the well born in verse 26.

The theme of God choosing the weak is old. He chose Israel because it was the smallest of the peoples, Deuteronomy 7:7. He chose Jacob and not Esau, Gideon with a tiny army, Judges 7, and David the youngest son, 1 Samuel 16:11 to 13. Mary sings of it in Luke 1:51 to 53, and Hannah before her in 1 Samuel 2:3 to 8. Paul places the cross as the final instance of a reversal that runs through the whole Bible.

The contrast between God's wisdom and human wisdom has roots in Job 28 and Proverbs. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, Proverbs 9:10, and the New Testament reads this as meaning that wisdom is found in a person, Christ, Colossians 2:3. The cross, as God's wisdom, is taken up again in 2:6 to 8 and in Romans 11:33 to 36.

The relation of cross and power recurs in 2 Corinthians 12:9, where the Lord says that His power is made perfect in weakness, and in 13:4, where Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by God's power. The thought also anticipates Philippians 2:5 to 11, in which the one who emptied Himself is the one exalted above every name.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul means to break the Corinthians' admiration for human cleverness by showing them how God Himself chose to work. He does this in two ways. First he argues from the message: if the cross is how God saves, then the strategies of eloquence and status have no part in it. Then he argues from the church's own membership: if God chose people of no standing, then there is no place for pride in standing.

He also wants to show that the cross is not a sad accident or a failure that God turned to good account. The wording of verse 21, that God was 'pleased' to save through what was preached, says that He designed it. The foolishness is by God's choice, and the wisdom that stands behind it is greater than the wisdom it overturns.

A third purpose is pastoral. The Corinthians were tempted to be embarrassed by the plainness of the gospel in a sophisticated city. Paul writes so that they will stop seeing the cross as something to explain away and begin to see it as the very thing in which they may take pride. The verses end with a command to boast, but in the Lord. It is a redirection of the instinct to boast, not its suppression.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The account of how Jews and Greeks respond, and the description of the make up of the Corinthian church, are descriptions of a time and place. Paul does not say that the church must always consist of the poor and uneducated, nor that learning is an enemy of faith. Verse 26 says 'not many,' and the New Testament has plenty of cases of educated and wealthy believers, from Luke to Lydia. What carries over is the principle that God's choice is not governed by human status.

The prescription is verse 31, boast only in the Lord, along with the implied call to rely on the message of the cross and not on techniques of impressing. Care is needed in applying it. The verses do not condemn thinking, study or good speech. Paul himself reasons carefully in all his letters, and in Acts 17 he addresses the Athenians with considerable skill. What he refuses is the idea that these things could carry the gospel's power or establish anyone's standing before God. Faith in a crucified Messiah will always look foolish to those who are perishing, and believers are not asked to hide that, but to hold to it.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by the foolishness and weakness of God in verse 25?

views.label: The cross as God's chosen means
views.case: God is not actually foolish or weak; Paul speaks of how the cross appears to human eyes. What the world judges as folly and weakness in the crucified Christ is in truth wiser and stronger than anything human, so the phrase is ironic praise of the cross.

views.label: A reversal of human categories
views.case: God deliberately works in a way that inverts human notions of wisdom and power, so that what looks least impressive accomplishes the greatest salvation, exposing the poverty of human standards.

debates.bearing: Both guard against any thought of real deficiency in God; the cross reveals a wisdom and power that surpass and humble every human measure.

debates.question: Does verse 21 mean human reason can never know anything true about God?

views.label: Fallen wisdom cannot save or truly know God
views.case: Paul's point is that the world, left to its own wisdom, failed to come to a saving knowledge of God and needs the gospel; it addresses the limits of wisdom for salvation, not every possible knowledge.

views.label: General revelation leaves people without excuse but not saved
views.case: Read with Romans 1, creation testifies to God so that people are without excuse, yet this witness does not bring saving knowledge; only the preached cross does that.

debates.bearing: The orthodox reading affirms that God is truly revealed in creation, yet holds that saving knowledge of God comes only through the cross, not through human wisdom.

debates.question: How should 'wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption' in verse 30 be read?

views.label: Three terms that explain the wisdom
views.case: The Greek has 'wisdom from God' followed by the three nouns, and many take the three as an explanation of what the wisdom is: Christ is our wisdom in that He is our righteousness, our holiness and our redemption. This fits the flow of the argument, since the paragraph is about what counts as wisdom.

views.label: Four distinct gifts
views.case: Others read the list as four separate benefits, with wisdom first, and see in the sequence a progression from justification to sanctification to final redemption. On this view the verse sums up the whole of salvation in four words.

debates.bearing: The readings differ in grammar and agree in substance. In either, Christ is Himself the gift and not merely the giver of gifts, so that a believer who has Him has everything the Corinthians sought elsewhere.

debates.question: Are the Corinthians' social origins in verse 26 evidence about the church's wealth?

views.label: Mostly poor and humble
views.case: Verse 26 says 'not many,' and the language of 'lowly and despised' in verse 28 suggests that most believers had little standing. The mention of slaves in 7:21 supports a church drawn largely from the lower ranks.

views.label: Mixed, with some of means
views.case: Some scholars point to Crispus, Gaius, Erastus and Stephanas as people of some standing, and to the conflicts at the Lord's Supper, 11:21 to 22, as evidence that the church included both rich and poor. On this view Paul is describing a general trend and not stating that no one had status.

debates.bearing: Paul's own words, 'not many,' leave room for both. The theological point is the same either way: the church did not owe its existence to the abilities of its members.

study.originalLanguages:
Several terms in these verses open up when they are read in Greek. The first is the pair of participles in verse 18, apollumenois, 'those who are perishing,' and sozomenois, 'those who are being saved.' Both are present tense. Paul describes two groups on a road, with one heading to destruction and the other being brought to safety, and the present tense says that the process is underway and has not yet reached its end. The same pair appears in 2 Corinthians 2:15 and 4:3. The word of the cross does not make people perish. It marks the direction they are already travelling, depending on how they hear it.

The second is skandalon, 'stumbling block,' in verse 23. The word originally meant the trigger of a trap or an obstacle on a path. Paul uses it of the crucified Messiah as something that Jews trip over, because it contradicts what they expected of a Messiah. In Romans 9:33 Paul quotes Isaiah for the same idea, that God lays in Zion a stone of stumbling. The cross is a trip for pride, not a lack of evidence for the mind.

The third is the perfect participle in the same verse, estauromenon, in 'Christ crucified.' The perfect tense does not describe an event that is over, but a state that continues. Paul preaches Christ as the one who was crucified and who remains the crucified one, whose wounds are part of who He is. The same form appears in 2:2 and Galatians 3:1. It matters that the church's message is not simply that He died but that this is how He is known.

The fourth is the verb eudokeo, 'was pleased,' in verse 21. It expresses the willing choice of God. The Father uses it of the Son at the baptism, Matthew 3:17, and Colossians 1:19 uses it for His pleasure to have all fullness dwell in Christ. The cross is not something God put up with. It is what pleased Him, and the phrase 'in the wisdom of God' at the start of verse 21 gives the reason for His pleasure.

The fifth is the phrase 'things that are not,' ta me onta, in verse 28, and the verb katargeo, 'to nullify,' that follows. The language is the language of creation. In Romans 4:17 Paul says that God 'calls into being what does not yet exist.' The Corinthians were nothing in the eyes of the world, and God made something of them, while what the world counted as something He made empty. The verb katargeo means to render inoperative, and the same verb is used for the rulers of this age 'coming to nothing' in 2:6.

The sixth is in verse 29, where the Greek says that 'no flesh' may boast, and the word sarx here is the creature in its weakness. 'In His presence,' enopion tou theou, is the language of a court. The sentence says that no human being will be able to stand before God and claim credit. Finally, in verse 30, the phrase 'because of Him you are in Christ Jesus' is literally 'from Him you are in Christ Jesus,' and the preposition marks source. The Corinthians' place in Christ comes from God and not from themselves, and the three words that follow, dikaiosune, hagiasmos and the redemption already named, show what that place gives.

typology.type: The weak and unlikely chosen, Deuteronomy 7:7 and 1 Samuel 16
typology.fulfillment: The LORD told Israel that He set His love on them not because they were more numerous but because they were the fewest of all peoples, Deuteronomy 7:7. He sent Samuel past the tall sons of Jesse to the youngest, 1 Samuel 16:11 to 13. The pattern is that God selects those who have nothing to boast about, so that the credit is plainly His. Paul reads the Corinthians as one more instance. The escalation is that the cross itself, the lowest point of apparent defeat, is the means by which God wins the greatest victory. The pattern still has a limit: the Old Testament examples ended in a king or a nation, and the cross ends in the redemption of people from every nation.

typology.type: The confounding of human counsel, Isaiah 29
typology.fulfillment: In Isaiah 29 the leaders of Jerusalem hide their plans and rely on their own cleverness, and God declares that the wisdom of the wise will vanish. The correspondence with Corinth is exact in structure. In both there is a community with confidence in its own counsel and a God who overturns it. Paul reads the cross as the supreme case, because the rulers of this age did not understand and crucified the Lord of glory, 2:8, and in doing so carried out God's plan. The type is extended from a political crisis to the whole human story. It still awaits completion, since 1 Corinthians 15:24 to 26 describes the final destruction of every rule and enemy.

typology.type: Ransom and release, Exodus 6 and Leviticus 25
typology.fulfillment: God promised to redeem Israel from Egypt 'with an outstretched arm,' Exodus 6:6, and the law provided that a kinsman could redeem a relative who had sold himself into servitude, Leviticus 25:47 to 49. Paul uses a word from this vocabulary when he says that Christ has become our redemption. The correspondence is deliverance by a price from a bondage that cannot be escaped by one's own effort. The escalation is that the one who pays is the one who is Himself the redemption, and the bondage is to sin and death. The type falls short in that Israel's redemption was from a human oppressor, while Christ's is from the powers that hold all humanity, as Hebrews 2:14 to 15 explains.

Jeremiah sets three things against the knowledge of the LORD: the wise should not boast in wisdom, the strong in strength, the rich in riches. Paul takes this pattern and applies it to the Corinthian situation, since the wise, the powerful and the well born are the three groups in verse 26. The correspondence is the replacement of every ground of boasting with a single one. The escalation is that knowing the LORD is now bound to Christ, who is made to us wisdom from God, and so the boast in the Lord is a boast in Christ. The pattern remains incomplete in that the full knowledge of the LORD that Jeremiah looked for belongs to the age to come, 1 Corinthians 13:12.

study.christ:
The paragraph leads to Christ by a series of striking claims, and each one grows from the one before. In verse 23 He is 'Christ crucified,' preached to a world that wanted something else. That is the first claim: the content of the message is a person and a particular event, not a general truth. Paul does not say that the Corinthians should think about God's love or about the value of suffering. He says that they should look at a man on a cross.

In verse 24 He is 'the power of God and the wisdom of God' for those who are called. The word 'power' is the opposite of what a crucifixion suggests, and 'wisdom' is the opposite of what it seems to show. Yet for those whose eyes have been opened, the cross reveals what the world cannot see, that the weakness of a dying man was the way God overcame sin and death. The two words in verse 24 answer the two demands of verse 22, signs and wisdom. The Jews wanted power and the Greeks wanted wisdom, and God gave both in the one thing they both rejected.

In verse 30 He is more than a teacher of wisdom. He has 'become for us wisdom from God.' The verb is the one for becoming, and it is in the past tense: at a point in history He became this for His people. The three nouns that follow give what the wisdom contains. He is our righteousness, which Romans 3:21 to 26 explains as the gift of right standing before God through His atoning death. He is our holiness, the sanctification already granted in 1:2 and developed in 6:11. And He is our redemption, the ransom that frees us from sin's slavery, with a final aspect in the resurrection of the body, Romans 8:23.

These verses also point to Christ as the one who was foolish and weak by choice. Paul says in 2 Corinthians 13:4 that He was crucified in weakness. Philippians 2:6 to 8 says that He emptied Himself and became obedient to death on a cross. The self-emptying was not a loss of divinity but the form of its display. That is why the foolishness of God can be wiser than men.

There is also a Christ-centred reading of 'in Christ Jesus' in verse 30. It is the sphere in which believers live and the source of everything they have. The Corinthians' status, which they had hoped to improve by wisdom and rhetoric, is settled by being in Him. This is a change from boasting about what one has to boasting about whose one is.

The paragraph ends with the Lord as the one in whom to boast. Jeremiah's 'Lord' is the LORD, and Paul's context makes the application to Christ plain, since the verse follows immediately on the description of Christ as everything. In 2 Corinthians 10:17 Paul quotes the same words, and in Galatians 6:14 he says, 'may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.' The cross is not only the subject of the message but the object of the boast.

A caution is in order. We should not read the 'foolish things' and 'weak things' of verse 27 as pictures of Christ. Paul says that God chose them, meaning the Corinthian believers. The link to Christ is that these people are in Him, and that God's way of dealing with them follows the pattern of what He did on the cross.
study.god:
The paragraph gives a picture of God that overturns an easy assumption, namely that the way God works must look impressive. He is the God who destroys the wisdom of the wise, verse 19, and makes foolish the wisdom of the world, verse 20. The verbs are active and the subject is God. The world is not left to find its own way out of its folly. He acts on it.

He is sovereign in election. Three times in verses 27 and 28 the sentence begins 'God chose,' and in verse 24 the people are 'called,' and in verse 30 it is 'because of Him' that they are in Christ. In each case the initiative is His. The people are not chosen for qualities they had, since the qualities named are the opposite of what the world admires. The doctrine of election is given here a pastoral shape. It does not exist to exclude but to humble, and it is told to a church for the purpose of ending boasting.

He is wise in a way that goes beyond human measure. Verse 21 says that the world through its wisdom 'did not know Him,' in the context of 'the wisdom of God.' That clause says that God had arranged the world so that human wisdom would meet its limit. Romans 1:20 says that creation shows God's eternal power and divine nature, and Romans 11:33 says that His ways are beyond tracing out. The cross is not an embarrassment to this wisdom but its centre.

He is strong in weakness. Verse 25 gives the paradox in its sharpest form. God has no real foolishness or weakness, and this is why His foolishness and weakness are wiser and stronger than man's best. The cross shows a God who does not need to prove His strength by displays of force, and whose power is shown in giving Himself.

He is the God who saves by grace and for His own glory. 'So that no one may boast in His presence' is the stated purpose of His method, and verse 31 gives the right response, boasting in Him. The glory of God and the good of His people are not in competition here. The church is humbled and God is glorified, and that is the pattern of salvation.

The tension the paragraph holds is between God's hiddenness and His self-disclosure. The world did not know Him by its wisdom, and yet He makes Himself known in the message of the cross. He is concealed from pride and revealed to faith. Paul does not resolve this by saying that revelation is partial, but by saying that the form of revelation is the cross, which can be seen as folly or as power depending on the heart of the one who looks.

For worship, the passage tells us to bring a particular kind of praise. It is not praise for what we have achieved, or for the knowledge we have gained, but for a rescue we could not have designed. It teaches the church to sing about a cross, and to do so without embarrassment.

crossReferences.note: God says that the people honour Him with their lips while their hearts are far away, and promises that the wisdom of the wise will vanish. This is the source of Paul's quotation in verse 19. Its original setting, a city leaning on its own schemes, shows that the folly of the wise is a theme older than the cross.

The prophet imagines the enemy's officials gone, and asks where the one who tallies and the one who weighs are. Paul's questions in verse 20, 'Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?' take up the same taunt. The comparison shows that he is speaking in the manner of the prophets, mocking the claims of human cleverness.

Jeremiah says the wise, the strong and the rich should not boast in those things, but whoever boasts should boast in knowing the LORD. Paul's final line in verse 31 comes from here, and the three categories in the Jeremiah passage match the three in verse 26. The whole paragraph reads as a commentary on this text.

Paul is not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. The sentence is the same claim as 1 Corinthians 1:18 in a calmer setting. Writing to Rome, a city that valued power, Paul uses the same word for power and says that the message others thought weak is the real force.

The Lord tells Paul that His grace is sufficient and His power is made perfect in weakness, and Paul concludes that when he is weak he is strong. This is the personal side of the paradox in verse 25. The pattern that holds for the cross also holds for the messenger.

Paul says he will never boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to him. The verse gives the positive form of the command in 1 Corinthians 1:31 and shows that the cross is the one thing in which he glories.

God 'calls into being what does not yet exist.' The words give the background to 'the things that are not' in verse 28. God's way of making the Corinthians His people is the same as His way of creating, and shows that nothing in them was the cause.

The rulers of this age did not understand God's hidden wisdom, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. The passage extends the argument of 1:18 to 31 by showing that the cross was the place where human wisdom made its worst mistake and God's plan was carried out.

Anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse. The verse explains why a crucified Messiah was a stumbling block to the Jews. Galatians 3:13 shows how Paul answers it, saying that Christ bore the curse for us, so that the shame of the cross becomes the means of blessing.

In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. The verse gives a parallel to verse 30, where Christ becomes our wisdom from God. The Corinthians were searching outside Him for what is found inside Him, and both letters say that wisdom is not a system but a person.

Mary sings that God has scattered the proud, brought down rulers from their thrones and lifted up the humble. The Magnificat gives the same reversal as verses 27 and 28, set in the language of Israel's hope. It shows that the pattern Paul finds at the cross was already part of the people's prayer.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is the story of a God who works through reversals. From the first chapters, the order that people expect is overturned. The younger is preferred to the older, the barren woman bears the promised child, a slave in Egypt becomes the deliverer, a shepherd boy becomes king. Each time, those who would have been left out are the ones God uses, and each time the aim is that He should receive the glory. In the Corinthian church the pattern appears once more, with a handful of ordinary people called into a company that worldly wisdom would have ignored.

The cross is the climax of that pattern. Everything that God had done through weakness and unlikely choices points toward the moment when the Son of God was nailed to a tree. At that point the powers of the world did what they thought was best and in so doing carried out God's plan, as 1 Corinthians 2:8 says. The Old Testament's repeated promise that God would confound the wise is shown in the crucifixion at full scale. The question that runs through the prophets, who has known the mind of the LORD, is answered in Christ.

The passage also answers the problem of the story's beginning. In Eden the pair listened to a voice that offered wisdom of their own, the knowledge of good and evil, and they fell. The attempt to be wise apart from God ruined them, and it has marked every generation since. Verses 18 to 31 describe the reversal: the wisdom that failed to find God is shown to be folly, and the wisdom that comes from God is given in a person. Where Adam grasped, Christ gave Himself up.

Looking forward, the passage prepares for the rest of the letter. Chapter 15 presents the resurrection as the vindication of the crucified one, and the pattern of weakness followed by power appears again in the picture of the body that is sown in weakness and raised in power, 15:43. The church's calling in the meantime is to live by the wisdom of the cross, in humility and love.

In the new creation there is no more boasting except in the Lord. Revelation 5:12 shows the Lamb who was slain receiving power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honour, glory and praise. All the things that the Corinthians sought on their own terms are given to the one who first gave them away. The people who were once the foolish, the weak and the lowly stand with Him, and the whole redeemed company says, as verse 31 foretold, that their one boast is the Lord.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the message of the cross in verse 18?

options.text: Foolishness to those perishing, but the power of God to those being saved.
options.note: The cross divides hearers: folly to some, saving power to others.

options.text: A wise philosophy that anyone can appreciate.
options.note: It is God's wisdom, but the world judges it folly, not an admired philosophy.

options.text: A message meant only for the educated elite.
options.note: The opposite; God chose the lowly, and the wise stumble over it.

options.text: A powerless story that saves no one.
options.note: To the saved it is the very power of God.

quiz.q: Why did God choose to save through what looks foolish and weak?

options.text: So that no one may boast in His presence, but only in the Lord.
options.note: Verses 29 to 31 give the purpose: to exclude human boasting and glorify God.

options.text: Because God could not find a more impressive way.
options.note: It is a deliberate, wise choice, not a limitation; His weakness is stronger than men.

options.text: To reward those who were already wise and powerful.
options.note: He chose the foolish and weak to shame the wise and strong.

options.text: Because appearances do not matter to God at all.
options.note: The point is a purposeful reversal to humble pride, not indifference.

quiz.q: How do Jews and Greeks respond to the preaching of Christ crucified?

options.text: It is a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but God's power and wisdom to the called.
options.note: Verses 22 to 24 capture both offenses and the saving reality for the called.

options.text: Both groups immediately welcome it as obvious truth.
options.note: Only those God calls receive it; to the rest it is offense or folly.

options.text: Only the Jews reject it, while all Greeks accept it.
options.note: Paul says it is folly to Gentiles and a stumbling block to Jews alike.

options.text: Everyone rejects it, and no one is saved.
options.note: To those who are called it is the power and wisdom of God.

quiz.q: What has Christ become for believers according to verse 30?

options.text: Wisdom from God: their righteousness, holiness, and redemption.
options.note: Christ is not merely the giver but the substance of every saving benefit.

options.text: A wise teacher who shows them how to save themselves.
options.note: He does not merely instruct; He becomes their righteousness and redemption.

options.text: One helpful source of wisdom among many others.
options.note: He is wisdom from God, the sole ground of their standing and freedom.

options.text: An example to admire but not a Savior to trust.
options.note: He is their redemption, purchased at the cost of Himself.

quiz.q: What is the one legitimate boast Paul leaves standing?

options.text: Boasting in the Lord.
options.note: Verse 31 cites Jeremiah: let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.

options.text: Boasting in the leader who taught you the most.
options.note: That is the very party pride Paul dismantles; the boast belongs to the Lord.

options.text: Boasting in your spiritual gifts and knowledge.
options.note: These are gifts of grace, not grounds for boasting before God.

options.text: Boasting in your wisdom and social standing.
options.note: God chose the lowly precisely so that such boasting is excluded.

questions: The cross looks like foolishness to the world but is the power of God. Where are you tempted to be embarrassed by the plain message of a crucified Savior?
God chose the lowly and unimpressive on purpose. How does it comfort you, and humble you, to know you were not chosen for your wisdom, strength, or status?
Christ has become your righteousness, holiness, and redemption. Which of these do you most need to rest in rather than trying to achieve it yourself?
Paul leaves only one boast standing, boasting in the Lord. What are you quietly boasting in instead, and what would it look like to transfer that boast to Christ?
The world still prizes cleverness and strength. How can you value the wisdom of the cross above the wisdom of the age in the decisions you make this week?

translationNotes.note: This quotes Isaiah 29:14, where God promises to confound the wisdom of the wise; Paul applies it to the way the cross empties human wisdom of its claim to reach God.
Christ crucified is a stumbling block, the Greek skandalon, to Jews; the shame of crucifixion and a suffering Messiah offended Jewish expectations of a triumphant deliverer.
The list righteousness, holiness, and redemption unpacks how Christ is wisdom from God; He is not only the giver of these but has become them for His people.
This condenses Jeremiah 9:23-24, where boasting in wisdom, might, and riches is forbidden and boasting in knowing the Lord is commended.
